chunks.title: What happens after you file a consumer complaint
chunks.text:
- **Admission.** The District Commission should ordinarily decide within 21 days whether to admit the complaint. It
  cannot reject it without hearing you, and if it does not decide in time, the complaint is treated as admitted
  (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 36(2) and (3)).
- **Mediation.** If a settlement looks possible, the Commission may ask both sides to agree in writing, within five
  days, to mediation (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 37(1)).
- **Order.** If your complaint is proved, the Commission orders relief such as replacement, refund with interest,
  compensation and costs.
- **Appeal.** Either side can appeal a District Commission order to the State Commission within 45 days of the order
  (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 41).
- **If the trader ignores the order.** Not complying with a Commission's order is punishable with imprisonment from
  one month up to three years, or a fine from Rs. 25,000 up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both (Consumer Protection Act, 2019,
  s. 72(1)).
chunks.header: What happens after you file a consumer complaint | consumer | guide

chunks.title: Filing a complaint with the District Consumer Commission
chunks.text:
**Which Commission.** It depends on the value of the goods or services you paid for: up to Rs. 50 lakh goes to the
District Commission; above Rs. 50 lakh and up to Rs. 2 crore to the State Commission; above Rs. 2 crore to the
National Commission (Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, rr. 3 to 5). Most everyday complaints go to the
District Commission.

**Which district.** You can file where the opposite party lives or does business or has a branch, where the cause of
action arose, or **where you live or work** (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 34(2)). So you can usually file in
your own district, even against a company based elsewhere.

**Who can file.** The consumer, a recognised consumer association, or several consumers with the same interest
together, with the Commission's permission (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 35(1)).

**How.** A complaint may be filed electronically (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 35(1), proviso), through the
e-Jagriti portal (e-jagriti.gov.in). It must be accompanied by the prescribed fee (s. 35(2)); check the current fee
on e-Jagriti for your claim amount.

You do not need a lawyer to file; you can present your own case.

sources.title: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021

chunks.header: Filing a complaint with the District Consumer Commission | consumer | guide

chunks.title: Online orders: what sellers and platforms must do about returns and refunds
chunks.text:
The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 put duties on online platforms and sellers:

- **No refusal to take back or refund** when goods or services are defective, deficient or spurious, not as
  advertised or agreed, or delivered late (except late delivery due to force majeure). This applies to sellers on a
  marketplace (E-Commerce Rules, 2020, r. 6(3)) and to platforms that sell their own inventory (r. 7(4)).
- **Grievance officer.** Every platform must appoint a grievance officer and show their name and contact details on
  the platform (r. 4(4)). The officer must acknowledge your complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month
  of receiving it (r. 4(5)). Marketplace sellers must do the same (r. 6(4)(b)).
- **Refunds** accepted by the platform must be paid within a reasonable time, as prescribed by the Reserve Bank of
  India or other applicable law (r. 4(10)).
- **Cancellation charges** cannot be imposed on you unless the platform bears similar charges when it cancels an
  order itself (r. 4(8)).

Keep the order ID, invoice, delivery proof, photos or videos of the product, and every chat or email with customer
care. Write to the grievance officer in writing and note the date: if there is no answer within a month, you have
a clear record for the next step.
chunks.header: Online orders: what sellers and platforms must do about returns and refunds | consumer | guide

chunks.title: National Consumer Helpline (1915): free help before going to a Commission
chunks.text:
The National Consumer Helpline (NCH), run by the Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India, helps resolve
consumer grievances with companies before a formal complaint.

- Toll-free: **1915** (8 AM to 8 PM) or 1800-11-4000
- WhatsApp: +91 88000 01915
- Online: consumerhelpline.gov.in → "Register Grievance"

Many large companies and platforms are "convergence partners" of the NCH, so a grievance registered there is sent to
the company directly. If the matter is not resolved, the next step is a complaint to the District Consumer
Commission on e-Jagriti.

Source: consumerhelpline.gov.in, checked 2026-11-21.
chunks.header: National Consumer Helpline (1915): free help before going to a Commission | consumer | practice

chunks.title: Refund, replacement or compensation for a bad product or service
chunks.text:
If you paid for goods or a service and got something defective, deficient, not as promised, or no refund that was
due, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 protects you. It applies to purchases made online or offline, including by
teleshopping and direct selling (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7), Explanation (b)).

You can complain about (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(6)):
- goods with a defect: a fault or shortcoming in quality, quantity, purity or standard (s. 2(10));
- a service with a deficiency: a shortcoming in quality or manner of performance, including negligence or
  deliberately withholding relevant information (s. 2(11));
- an unfair trade practice, or being charged more than the displayed, fixed or agreed price.

If the complaint is proved, a Consumer Commission can order the trader to remove the defect, replace the goods,
return the price with interest, pay compensation for loss or injury, pay punitive damages, and pay your costs
(Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 39(1)).

Usual path: complain to the seller (and the platform's grievance officer) → National Consumer Helpline 1915 →
complaint to the District Consumer Commission, which can be filed online on e-Jagriti.
chunks.header: Refund, replacement or compensation for a bad product or service | consumer | guide

chunks.title: Time limit for a consumer complaint
chunks.text:
A Consumer Commission will not admit a complaint unless it is filed within **two years** from the date the cause of
action arose (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 69(1)). The cause of action is usually when the defect appeared, the
service failed, or the refund was refused.

A late complaint can still be heard if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and the Commission records its
reasons for accepting it (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 69(2)). Do not rely on this: file within two years.
chunks.header: Time limit for a consumer complaint | consumer | guide

chunks.title: Are you a "consumer" under the law?
chunks.text:
You are a consumer if you bought goods, or hired or used a service, for a price that was paid or promised, fully or
in part, including in instalments (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7)). Someone who uses the goods or service
with the buyer's approval, such as a family member, also counts.

You are **not** a consumer if you bought the goods for resale or for a commercial purpose, or used the service for a
commercial purpose. Buying something to earn your own livelihood by self-employment is not a commercial purpose
(Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7), Explanation (a)).

Online purchases count: buying goods or hiring services includes transactions made online or through electronic
means, teleshopping, direct selling or multi-level marketing (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7),
Explanation (b)).
chunks.header: Are you a "consumer" under the law? | consumer | guide

chunks.title: What a landlord may deduct from the deposit
chunks.text:
What can be deducted depends on your rental agreement. Read its clauses on the deposit, notice period, painting,
repairs and unpaid bills.

Under contract law, a party who breaks a contract must compensate only the loss that naturally arises from that
breach; remote or indirect losses are not compensated (Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 73). So a landlord can
generally deduct, for example, unpaid rent or the cost of real damage that you caused, but should be able to show
what the loss was. If the agreement names a fixed amount payable for a breach (for example, a penalty for leaving
without notice), the landlord can claim only reasonable compensation up to that amount, not automatically the whole
of it (Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 74).

Practical steps:
- Ask the landlord for an itemised list of deductions with bills or photos.
- Compare each deduction with the agreement.
- Pay or accept only what the agreement and the evidence support, and dispute the rest in writing.
chunks.header: What a landlord may deduct from the deposit | deposit | guide

chunks.title: Evidence to collect for a deposit dispute
chunks.text:
Collect these before you send a demand or a notice. Keep copies; give originals to no one.

- **Rental agreement**, including any renewal, and the clause on the deposit and notice period.
- **Proof that you paid the deposit**: bank transfer statement, UPI screenshot, cheque details or a signed receipt.
- **Proof of rent payments**, to show nothing is due.
- **Proof that you moved out on time**: your notice to vacate, the landlord's reply, the date you handed over keys.
- **Condition of the home**: photos or video on moving in and moving out, with dates.
- **All messages** with the landlord or agent about the deposit, repairs and deductions.
- **Bills you paid** (electricity, water, maintenance) up to the day you left.

If something is missing, say so in your notice instead of guessing; a notice with wrong facts weakens your case.
chunks.header: Evidence to collect for a deposit dispute | deposit | practice

chunks.title: Is there a legal limit on the security deposit in Karnataka?
chunks.text:
LawBuddy's sources contain no legal limit on the size of a security deposit for homes in Karnataka.

The Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 does not set a maximum deposit. Where the Act talks about "deposit", it means a tenant
depositing rent with the Controller when the landlord refuses to accept it (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 17). The
Karnataka Rent (Amendment) Act, 2025 changed the Controller's powers and the offences and penalties under the Act
(for example, fines in place of imprisonment); it did not add a deposit limit (Karnataka Rent (Amendment) Act, 2025,
ss. 2 to 5).

Claims online of a "two-month deposit cap" in Karnataka do not come from these laws. If someone relies on a deposit
cap, ask them which law and section it comes from.

So the amount of the deposit, and when it must be returned, is whatever your rental agreement says.
chunks.header: Is there a legal limit on the security deposit in Karnataka? | deposit | guide

chunks.title: Getting your security deposit back from a landlord in Karnataka
chunks.text:
A security deposit is money you gave the landlord to hold, to be returned when you leave. Whether you get it back,
and how much may be deducted, is decided mainly by your rental agreement.

For most rented homes in Karnataka today, a dispute over a deposit is a dispute about a contract. The Karnataka
Rent Act, 1999 does not apply to many homes: it excludes premises whose rent is above a low limit and buildings
constructed or substantially renovated in the last fifteen years (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 2(3)). When the
landlord keeps money the agreement says must be returned, that is a breach of contract, and the person who suffers
from a breach can claim compensation for the loss it caused (Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 73).

The usual path, from cheapest to most formal:
1. Ask in writing (message or email) for the refund, with a date to pay by.
2. Send a legal notice that sets out the facts, the amount and a deadline.
3. Try settlement through a Lok Adalat via the District Legal Services Authority.
4. File a civil suit to recover the money.
chunks.header: Getting your security deposit back from a landlord in Karnataka | deposit | guide

chunks.title: Does the Karnataka Rent Act apply to your rented home?
chunks.text:
The Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 regulates rent and eviction, but only for some premises. Its main rules (Chapters I to
III and V to VIII) apply in the areas listed in its First Schedule: Part A covers the cities constituted under the
Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976 and a radius of three kilometres around them; Part B covers areas within
City Municipal Councils (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 2(1) and First Schedule).

Even in those areas, the Act does not apply to (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 2(3)):
- premises whose deemed rent or standard rent is above Rs. 3,500 a month in a Part A area, or above Rs. 2,000 a
  month in any other area;
- premises constructed or substantially renovated in the last fifteen years, counted from completion;
- premises used for non-residential purposes, except small commercial premises of up to fourteen square metres;
- premises of the Central or State Government, a local authority, a religious or charitable institution or a Wakf,
  and buildings of co-operative societies.

In practice, most rented flats and houses in Bengaluru and other cities pay more than these limits, so the Act
usually does not apply. The tenancy is then governed by the rental agreement and general contract law.
chunks.header: Does the Karnataka Rent Act apply to your rented home? | deposit | guide

chunks.title: If the Karnataka Rent Act does apply to your home
chunks.text:
For the smaller group of tenancies the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 covers (low rent, older buildings, in listed areas):

- A tenancy must be by a written agreement (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 4).
- A tenant who pays rent, other charges or an advance is entitled to a signed written receipt from the landlord
  (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, s. 16(2)).
- If the landlord refuses to accept rent, the tenant may deposit it with the Controller (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999,
  s. 17).
- If a tenant paid any sum to the landlord in breach of the Act, the Controller may order the landlord to refund
  it, or adjust it against rent, on an application made within one year of the payment (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999,
  s. 15).
- Controllers are officers appointed by the State Government to decide these matters (Karnataka Rent Act, 1999,
  s. 23).

Whether the Act applies to a particular home turns on its rent, age and location; a lawyer or the DLSA can confirm.
chunks.header: If the Karnataka Rent Act does apply to your home | deposit | guide

chunks.title: Steps to recover a deposit, from demand to court
chunks.text:
1. **Written demand.** Message or email the landlord asking for the deposit by a clear date (for example, 7 days).
   Keep the reply, or the lack of one.
2. **Legal notice.** If there is no payment, send a legal notice by registered post (and email or WhatsApp) stating
   the facts, the amount due, the deadline and that you will take legal action. LawBuddy can draft one for you to
   review and sign.
3. **Lok Adalat (settlement).** The District Legal Services Authority can take up a dispute that is not yet in court
   on the application of one party and refer it to a Lok Adalat (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s. 20). A
   settlement there becomes an award that is final and binding, with no appeal (Legal Services Authorities Act,
   1987, s. 21). It only works if the landlord agrees to settle.
4. **Civil suit.** If nothing else works, file a suit to recover the money. Which court hears it depends on the
   amount and the place, so ask a lawyer or your DLSA before filing.

Time limit: a suit for compensation for breach of a contract must generally be filed within three years from when
the contract is broken (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Article 55). Act early; the exact start date depends on
your facts.
chunks.header: Steps to recover a deposit, from demand to court | deposit | guide

chunks.title: Free legal aid: who qualifies and where to ask
chunks.text:
The Constitution directs the State to provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of
economic or other disabilities (Constitution of India, Article 39A). The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 puts
this into practice.

You are entitled to free legal services to file or defend a case if you are (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987,
s. 12):
- a woman or a child;
- a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe;
- a person with a disability;
- an industrial workman;
- a victim of trafficking, or of a mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or
  industrial disaster;
- in custody; or
- a person whose annual income is below the limit set by the State Government (for cases in courts other than the
  Supreme Court).

The Authority must also be satisfied that you have a prima facie case (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987,
s. 13(1)).

**Where to ask:** the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at your district court, the Taluk Legal Services
Committee, the Karnataka State Legal Services Authority (kslsa.kar.nic.in), or the NALSA helpline **15100**
(toll-free). Ask them for the current income limit in Karnataka.
chunks.header: Free legal aid: who qualifies and where to ask | general | guide

chunks.title: What a legal notice is and why to send one
chunks.text:
A legal notice is a formal letter telling the other side what they owe or must do, by when, and that you will take
legal action if they do not. For deposit, refund and salary disputes, none of the laws in LawBuddy's sources requires
one before going to a Consumer Commission, a wage authority or a Lok Adalat, but it is a good first formal step
because:

- it often makes the other side pay or settle, at little cost;
- it creates a dated record that you demanded payment, which helps prove your case and when the dispute began;
- it forces you to set out the facts and the amount clearly.

A good notice states: who you are and who it is addressed to; the facts in date order; the amount or action
demanded; a deadline (commonly 15 days); and what you will do if they do not comply. It should be factual and
polite, with no threats beyond lawful action, and no facts you cannot prove.

Send it by registered post or speed post with acknowledgement, and also by email or WhatsApp. Keep the postal receipt
and tracking record. A notice can be sent by you yourself or through a lawyer; one sent through a lawyer often
carries more weight.
chunks.header: What a legal notice is and why to send one | general | practice

chunks.title: Lok Adalat: settling a dispute without a long court case
chunks.text:
Lok Adalats are organised by the State and District Legal Services Authorities (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987,
s. 19). They settle disputes by compromise.

- **Before a case is filed:** one party can apply to the Legal Services Authority to have a dispute that is not yet in
  court referred to a Lok Adalat (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s. 20(2)). The other side is heard before
  the matter is referred.
- **Result:** if both sides settle, the award is treated as a decree of a civil court, is final and binding on all
  parties, and no appeal lies against it. If a pending court case is settled this way, the court fee paid is
  refunded (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s. 21).
- **If there is no settlement,** the parties are advised to seek their remedy in court (s. 20(6)).

Lok Adalat suits disputes where the other side may be willing to pay something to close the matter, such as a
deposit or dues dispute. Contact your District Legal Services Authority to ask about the next Lok Adalat.
chunks.header: Lok Adalat: settling a dispute without a long court case | general | guide

chunks.title: Laws that have been replaced
chunks.text:
Many websites and older documents still quote laws that have been repealed. Do not rely on them:

- The **Consumer Protection Act, 1986** was repealed by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (s. 107). Consumer
  complaints now go to District, State and National Consumer **Commissions** (earlier called Forums).
- The **Payment of Wages Act, 1936**, the **Minimum Wages Act, 1948**, the **Payment of Bonus Act, 1965** and the
  **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** were repealed by the Code on Wages, 2019 (s. 69).
- The **Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961** was replaced by the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 (s. 70).
- The **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**, the **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)** and the **Indian Evidence Act** were
  replaced in 2024 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya
  Adhiniyam. Criminal matters are outside LawBuddy's scope; see a lawyer.
chunks.header: Laws that have been replaced | general | guide

chunks.title: When you need a real lawyer, and what LawBuddy does not cover
chunks.header: When you need a real lawyer, and what LawBuddy does not cover | general | practice

chunks.title: Filing a wage claim under the Code on Wages
chunks.text:
The government appoints authorities (officers not below the rank of Gazetted Officer) to hear and decide claims under
the Code (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 45(1)). In Karnataka, ask the Labour Department which officer hears these
claims for your area.

- **Who can file:** you, a registered trade union you belong to, or an Inspector-cum-Facilitator. One application
  can cover many employees of the same establishment (s. 45(4) and (5)).
- **Time limit:** within **three years** from when the claim arises; a later application may be accepted if you show
  sufficient cause (s. 45(6)).
- **What you can get:** the amount due, plus compensation of up to **ten times** the claim, depending on the
  circumstances. The authority should try to decide within three months (s. 45(2)).
- **If the employer still does not pay:** the authority sends a recovery certificate to the Collector or District
  Magistrate, who recovers it as arrears of land revenue (s. 45(3)).
- **Who is responsible:** the employer; if the employer fails, the company, firm or proprietor of the establishment
  (s. 43).
- **Appeal:** either side may appeal the authority's order within 90 days (s. 49(1)).
chunks.header: Filing a wage claim under the Code on Wages | salary | guide

chunks.title: Evidence to collect for unpaid salary
chunks.text:
- **Proof you were employed**: offer or appointment letter, ID card, joining email, PF/ESI number, or messages from
  your manager.
- **Proof of salary**: payslips, bank statements showing earlier salary credits, or the salary stated in the offer.
- **Proof of work in the unpaid period**: attendance records, timesheets, emails or work you submitted.
- **Exit documents** if you left: resignation email, acceptance, relieving letter, last working day.
- **Every message** asking for payment, and any promise the employer made to pay.
- **Who the employer is**: the company or proprietor's legal name and address, from the offer letter, payslip or
  GST/website details. You need the correct name for a notice or claim.

Write down the months unpaid and the exact amount for each month; LawBuddy will put them in a table.
chunks.header: Evidence to collect for unpaid salary | salary | practice

chunks.title: Unpaid salary or final dues: your rights
chunks.text:
Wages are governed by the Code on Wages, 2019, which replaced the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act,
1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 69).

"Employee" under the Code covers anyone employed on wages by an establishment to do skilled, semi-skilled, unskilled,
manual, operational, supervisory, managerial, administrative, technical or clerical work, except apprentices and
members of the Armed Forces (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 2(k)).

**When wages must be paid** (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 17(1)):
- daily workers: at the end of the shift;
- weekly: on the last working day of the week;
- fortnightly: before the end of the second day after the fortnight ends;
- **monthly: before the seventh day of the next month ends.**

**When you leave.** If you resign, or are removed, dismissed or retrenched, or the establishment closes, the wages due
to you must be paid **within two working days** (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 17(2)).

The government may set other time limits in some circumstances (s. 17(3)). Karnataka's own rules under the Code were
still in draft when LawBuddy's sources were collected, so check with the Karnataka Labour Department for procedure.
chunks.header: Unpaid salary or final dues: your rights | salary | guide

chunks.title: Steps to recover unpaid salary
chunks.text:
1. **Written demand** to HR or the owner by email, listing the unpaid months and amounts and a date to pay by.
2. **Legal notice** if there is no payment: facts, amounts, the legal deadline for payment, and a warning that you
   will file a claim. LawBuddy can draft one for you to review and sign.
3. **Wage claim** before the authority appointed under the Code on Wages (ask the Karnataka Labour Department which
   officer hears claims for your area), within three years (Code on Wages, 2019, s. 45(6)). This is usually faster and cheaper than court, and can award compensation
   of up to ten times the claim (s. 45(2)).
4. **Civil suit** as an alternative: a suit for wages must be filed within three years from when the wages became
   due (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Article 7). Talk to a lawyer or the DLSA before choosing this route.

Free help: industrial workmen are among those entitled to free legal services (see "Free legal aid").
chunks.header: Steps to recover unpaid salary | salary | guide

chunks.title: Indian Contract Act, 1872, sections 73 and 74 (text)
chunks.text:
**Section 73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract.** When a contract has been broken, the
party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation
for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach,
or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it.

Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

**Section 74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for.** When a contract has been broken,
if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any
other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage
or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable
compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
chunks.header: Indian Contract Act, 1872, sections 73 and 74 (text) | deposit | statute

chunks.title: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, rules 4(5), 4(10) and 6(3) (text)
chunks.text:
**Rule 4(5).** Every e-commerce entity shall ensure that the grievance officer referred to in sub-rule (4)
acknowledges the receipt of any consumer complaint within forty-eight hours and redresses the complaint within one
month from the date of receipt of the complaint.

**Rule 4(10).** Every e-commerce entity shall effect all payments towards accepted refund requests of the consumers
as prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India or any other competent authority under any law for the time being in
force, within a reasonable period of time, or as prescribed under applicable laws.

**Rule 6(3).** No seller offering goods or services through a marketplace e-commerce entity shall refuse to take
back goods, or withdraw or discontinue services purchased or agreed to be purchased, or refuse to refund
consideration, if paid, if such goods or services are defective, deficient or spurious, or if the goods or services
are not of the characteristics or features as advertised or as agreed to, or if such goods or services are delivered
late from the stated delivery schedule: Provided that in the case of late delivery, this sub-rule shall not be
applied if such late delivery was due to force majeure.
chunks.header: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, rules 4(5), 4(10) and 6(3) (text) | consumer | statute

chunks.title: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, rules 3 to 5 (text)
chunks.text:
**3. Jurisdiction of District Commission.** Subject to the other provisions of the Act and in pursuance of proviso to
sub-section (1) of section 34 of the Act, the District Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain complaints
where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees.

**4. Jurisdiction of State Commission.** ... the State Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain complaints
where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore
rupees.

**5. Jurisdiction of National Commission.** ... the National Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain
complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration, exceeds two crore rupees.

sources.title: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021

chunks.header: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, rules 3 to 5 (text) | consumer | statute

chunks.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sections 34(2), 35(1) proviso and 69 (text)
chunks.text:
**Section 34(2).** A complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose
jurisdiction,
(a) the opposite party or each of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the
institution of the complaint, ordinarily resides or carries on business or has a branch office or personally works
for gain; or
(b) any of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint,
actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business or has a branch office, or personally works for gain,
provided that in such case the permission of the District Commission is given; or
(c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises; or
(d) the complainant resides or personally works for gain.

**Section 35(1), proviso.** Provided that the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such
manner as may be prescribed.

**Section 69.** (1) The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a
complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a complaint may be entertained after the period specified
in sub-section (1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National
Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period:
Provided that no such complaint shall be entertained unless the District Commission or the State Commission or the
National Commission, as the case may be, records its reasons for condoning such delay.
chunks.header: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sections 34(2), 35(1) proviso and 69 (text) | consumer | statute

chunks.title: Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Articles 22, 55 and 113 (text)
chunks.text:
| Article | Description of suit | Period of limitation | Time from which period begins to run |
|---|---|---|---|

chunks.title: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, sections 12 and 21, and Constitution Article 39A (text)
chunks.text:
**Constitution of India, Article 39A. Equal justice and free legal aid.** The State shall secure that the operation
of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal
aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are
not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

**Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, section 12.** Every person who has to file or defend a case shall be entitled
to legal services under this Act if that person is: (a) a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; (b) a
victim of trafficking in human beings or beggar as referred in article 23 of the Constitution; (c) a woman or a
child; (d) a person with disability ...; (e) a person under circumstances of undeserved want such as being a victim of
a mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster; or (f) an
industrial workman; or (g) in custody ...; or (h) in receipt of annual income less than rupees nine thousand or such
other higher amount as may be prescribed by the State Government, if the case is before a court other than the
Supreme Court ...

**Section 21(1)-(2).** Every award of the Lok Adalat shall be deemed to be a decree of a civil court ... Every award
made by a Lok Adalat shall be final and binding on all the parties to the dispute, and no appeal shall lie to any
court against the award.

chunks.title: Karnataka Rent Act, 1999, section 2(3)(e) to (g) (text)
chunks.text:
**Section 2(3).** Nothing contained in this Act shall apply, ...

(e) to any premises, deemed rent on the date of commencement of this Act or the standard rent of which exceeds,
(i) three thousand five hundred rupees per month in any area referred to in part A of the first schedule; and
(ii) two thousand rupees per month in any other area.

(f) to any premises constructed or substantially renovated, either before or after the commencement of this Act for
a period of fifteen years from the date of completion of such construction or substantial renovation.
Explanation-I. A premises may be said to be substantially renovated if not less than seventy-five percent of the
premises is built new in accordance with the criteria prescribed for determining the extent of renovation.

(g) to any premises used for non-residential purpose but excluding premises having a plinth area of not exceeding
fourteen square meters used for commercial purpose.

**First Schedule, Part A.** Areas within the limits of Cities constituted under the Karnataka Municipal Corporation
Act 1976 and within a radius of three kilometres from the limit of the said cities. **Part B.** Areas within the
limits of the City Municipal Councils constituted under Karnataka Municipalities Act 1964.

chunks.title: Code on Wages, 2019, section 17 (text)
chunks.text:
**17. Time limit for payment of wages.** (1) The employer shall pay or cause to be paid wages to the employees,
engaged on,
(i) daily basis, at the end of the shift;
(ii) weekly basis, on the last working day of the week, that is to say, before the weekly holiday;
(iii) fortnightly basis, before the end of the second day after the end of the fortnight;
(iv) monthly basis, before the expiry of the seventh day of the succeeding month.
(2) Where an employee has been, (i) removed or dismissed from service; or (ii) retrenched or has resigned from
service, or became unemployed due to closure of the establishment, the wages payable to him shall be paid within two
working days of his removal, dismissal, retrenchment or, as the case may be, his resignation.
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), the appropriate Government may,
provide any other time limit for payment of wages where it considers reasonable having regard to the circumstances
under which the wages are to be paid.
(4) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall affect any time limit for payment of wages provided
in any other law for the time being in force.

chunks.title: Code on Wages, 2019, section 45 (text, extract)
chunks.text:
**45. Claims under Code and procedure thereof.** (1) The appropriate Government may, by notification, appoint one or
more authorities, not below the rank of a Gazetted Officer, to hear and determine the claims which arises under the
provisions of this Code.
(2) The authority appointed under sub-section (1), while deciding the claim under that sub-section, may order,
having regard to the circumstances under which the claim arises, the payment of compensation in addition to the claim
determined, which may extend to ten times of the claim determined and endeavour shall be made by the authority to
decide the claim within a period of three months.
(3) If an employer fails to pay the claim determined and compensation ordered to be paid under sub-section (2), the
authority shall issue a certificate of recovery to the Collector or District Magistrate of the district where the
establishment is located who shall recover the same as arrears of land revenue and remit the same to the authority
for payment to the concerned employee.
(4) Any application before the authority for claim referred to in sub-section (1) may be filed by, (a) the employee
concerned; or (b) any Trade Union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 of which the employee is a member; or
(c) the Inspector-cum-Facilitator.
(6) The application under sub-section (4) may be filed within a period of three years from the date on which claims
referred to in sub-section (1) arises: Provided that the authority referred to in sub-section (1) may, entertain the
application after three years on sufficient cause being shown by the applicant for such delay.
